claims.claim: A written WotC house style guide does exist for the 5e era: 'D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing', Version 1.04a ©2013 Wizards of the Coast, distributed to freelancers/Adventurers League authors and later bundled on the DMs Guild; it governs mechanics of style, not prose voice.
claims.source: Wizards of the Coast, D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing v1.04a (PDF, 9 pp.)
claims.quote: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing

claims.claim: The house style rests on the Chicago Manual of Style 16th ed. and Merriam-Webster's Collegiate 11th ed., with the guide covering only D&D-specific departures.
claims.source: Wizards of the Coast, D&D Style Guide v1.04a
claims.quote: The Chicago Manual of Style, 16th edition

claims.claim: Rules text is written in the second person, which the guide presents as the standard way to achieve gender neutrality; singular 'they' is banned outside dialogue and 'he/she' alternation is forbidden.
claims.source: Wizards of the Coast, D&D Style Guide v1.04a
claims.quote: achieve gender neutrality by writing in the second person

claims.claim: 5e inline subheads (heading 4) end in a period rather than the colon used in earlier editions, e.g. 'Keen Senses. You have proficiency...'
claims.source: Wizards of the Coast, D&D Style Guide v1.04a
claims.quote: followed by terminal punctuation, not a colon

claims.claim: The guide fixes a verb list for mechanics: you 'make' a saving throw that 'succeeds or fails', attacks 'hit or miss', you 'deal' and 'take' damage, 'regain' hit points, and 'must succeed on' (not 'must make') a check.
claims.source: Wizards of the Coast, D&D Style Guide v1.04a
claims.quote: You make a saving throw, and it succeeds or fails.

claims.claim: The only prose-tone guidance is a 'High Fantasy' paragraph: epic scope, teamwork over lone heroes, humour or tragedy permitted only if they would not seem out of place in Lord of the Rings or Game of Thrones.
claims.source: Wizards of the Coast, D&D Style Guide v1.04a
claims.quote: ring wraiths aren't used for gags

claims.claim: The Dungeon house template keys each encounter as header/EL, mandatory Read-Aloud Text first, then General Description, Creature(s), Tactics, Development and Treasure, with adventures of 5,000–15,000 words and about 10,000 preferred.
claims.source: Paizo/Dungeon staff, Dungeon Submission Guidelines (PDF)
claims.quote: This section generally precedes the other entries of an encounter

claims.claim: The WotC House Style Guide bundle circulated to freelancers is summarised as: focus on the characters, include a credible threat, focus on the here and now and omit verbose backstories.
claims.source: Mike Shea, 'On Writing Adventures', Sly Flourish, 2019-06-17
claims.quote: Focus on the here and now. Omit verbose backstories.

claims.claim: McKenzie treats read-aloud text as the adventure's 'at rise' stage direction, typographically set apart and read verbatim, and dates its first appearance to The Hidden Shrine of Tamoachan.
claims.source: Brian McKenzie, 'D&D Adventures as Tragedy', Analog Game Studies, 2023-12-18
claims.quote: hints of what may be done are given in this text

claims.claim: Grouling Cover argues second-person address pulls players directly into the storyworld, situating and immersing them, drawing on Fludernik's narratology of second-person texts.
claims.source: Jennifer Grouling Cover, The Creation of Narrative in Tabletop Role-Playing Games (2010), pp. 21, 85
claims.quote: pulling them directly into the storyworld

claims.claim: Hines finds Tomb of Annihilation's text repeatedly uses 'tribal', 'exotic' and 'savage', and its Port Nyanzaru read-aloud leans on vague stereotypes (dinosaurs, bright clothing, click languages) rather than specific cultural detail.
claims.source: Mark Hines, Analog Game Studies, 2023-03-19
claims.quote: heavy, characteristic accent

claims.claim: Hines notes DM-facing text instructs voicing Chultans with a heavy accent and tongue clicks, and reads background wording like 'correctly ascertain its original purpose' as prose that frames ruins as needing outsider validation.
claims.source: Mark Hines, Analog Game Studies, 2023-03-19
claims.quote: correctly ascertain its original purpose

claims.claim: Hewitt shows Curse of Strahd's Death House read-aloud builds gothic atmosphere through decay adjectives (moldy, rusty, gaunt, pale-faced, voluminous) in present-tense third-person description.
claims.source: Meghan Hewitt, Analog Game Studies, 2024-12-15
claims.quote: festooned with moldy skeletons

claims.claim: Jara analyses rulebooks as framing devices whose covers, prologues, epilogues and embedded fiction shape play; storytelling-game books open with atmospheric prologue fiction, whereas the 1974 D&D booklets used such framing far less.
claims.source: David Jara, 'A Closer Look at the (Rule-) Books', International Journal of Role-Playing 4 (2013)
claims.quote: notoriously less prominent in early TRPGs

claims.claim: Jara coins 'genesic framing' for rulebook text that discloses its own framing and incites players to produce further text, which he says accounts for the medium's persistence.
claims.source: David Jara, IJRP 4 (2013)
claims.quote: what I have called genesic framing

claims.claim: Macdonell argues the 1978 Tomb of Horrors' scripted descriptions and its illustration booklet are dissonant, producing interpretive ambiguity, and that later editions removed the visual assets (abstract only; full text paywalled).
claims.source: Cameron Macdonell, 'Tomes and Tombs', Games and Culture, 2025
claims.quote: visual–textual dissonance produces interpretive ambiguity

claims.claim: The community term 'High Gygaxian' (coined by Maliszewski) names Gygax's archaic, thesaurus-driven diction ('perforce', 'antithesis of weal'), long multi-clause sentences and baroque tone, fullest in the 1979 DMG and Vault of the Drow.
claims.source: James Maliszewski, 'High Gygaxian', Grognardia, 2009-02-19
claims.quote: a platinum word when one worth a copper would do

claims.claim: Akrasia argues AD&D's Latinate vocabulary ('milieu', 'dweomer', 'phantasm', 'eldritch') made difficulty part of the appeal, and that later TSR simplification of the language reduced that cachet.
claims.source: Akrasia, Akratic Wizardry, 2013-03-18
claims.quote: you had to be smarter than average to understand it

claims.claim: A close reading of S1 Tomb of Horrors finds elevated verbs ('precipitated' for dropped), room text that mixes mechanics with narrative so it needs re-reading, yet short punchy details.
claims.source: Gus L, Dungeon of Signs, 2017-04-21
claims.quote: Gygax was good at short punchy bits of detail

claims.claim: The 1977 Monster Manual placed stat lines on the same page as descriptions, and Ed Greenwood criticised Fiend Folio entries for offering strange appearances with no depth to their listings.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Monsters in Dungeons & Dragons'
claims.quote: there is no depth to their listings

claims.claim: Wikipedia credits The Hidden Shrine of Tamoachan as the first D&D adventure with boxed read-aloud text, but the citation is a 2017 blog post by Merric Blackman, not a scholarly source.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'The Hidden Shrine of Tamoachan'
claims.quote: the first D&D adventure to use boxed

claims.claim: Reviewers cited on Wikipedia find Xanathar's marginal quips too modern in register, sounding like a cranky Redditor rather than a fantasy crime lord.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Xanathar's Guide to Everything' (citing Charlie Hall, Polygon)
claims.quote: feels a bit too modern

claims.feature: house style guide (community says none published, 2024 rules)
claims.claim: Paul Hughes built an unofficial 2024 style guide because no official one for the 2024 rules is available to the public.
claims.source: Blog of Holding — Unofficial D&D 2024 Style Guide (Paul Hughes, 2025-01-07)
claims.quote: it annoys me not to have an official style guide

claims.claim: Kobold Press ran a 'Designing with Style' series that explicitly 'breaks down the official 5th-edition style guide', quoting its Common Pitfalls section verbatim — evidence the guide was public and treated as canonical by third-party 5e designers.
claims.source: Kobold Press — Designing with Style: Ability Checks and Saving Throws (Hannah Rose, 2019-05-31)
claims.quote: breaks down the official 5th-edition style guide

claims.claim: v1.04a forbids 'they'/'their' as singular pronouns except in dialogue; v1.08a reverses this 'in a departure from our past usage' but tells writers to rely on it only when no pleasing alternative exists.
claims.source: Wizards of the Coast — D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (©2018, 'updated January 2019'; PDF mirror)
claims.quote: but don't abuse this liberty

claims.claim: Inline subheads (heading 4) end with terminal punctuation, not a colon — 'Keen Senses. You have proficiency…' — and are set in bold italics; bolded stat-block fields are a different thing.
claims.source: Wizards of the Coast — D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.04a (©2013; PDF hosted by the Adventurers League blog)
claims.quote: followed by terminal punctuation, not a colon

claims.feature: no weeks or months in rules
claims.claim: Because a Realms week is a tenday, rules durations are given in days, never weeks or months (years are allowed).
claims.source: Wizards of the Coast — D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.04a (©2013; PDF hosted by the Adventurers League blog)
claims.quote: say a game effect lasts for 7 days

claims.claim: v1.08a adds a diction rule: avoid 'fellowship' for adventuring groups because D&D companies are 'often fractious or more mercenary'; use group, band, company or especially 'party'.
claims.source: Wizards of the Coast — D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (©2018, 'updated January 2019'; PDF mirror)
claims.quote: often fractious or more mercenary

claims.claim: v1.08a: write 'priest', 'actor', 'god' regardless of gender; '-ess' forms only in in-world titles.
claims.source: Wizards of the Coast — D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (©2018, 'updated January 2019'; PDF mirror)
claims.quote: Avoid gender-specific suffixes whenever possible

claims.feature: in-world tenday rule vs WotC practice
claims.claim: A poster notes the style guide bans 'week' in favor of 'tenday' while WotC's own hardcovers violate the rule — house style is aspirational, not uniformly applied.
claims.source: EN World — DMsGuild: D&D Style-Guides give a unique insight into the game (thread, 2018-11-25)

claims.claim: A community-compiled 5e writer's guide: 'Write in the present tense', avoiding 'will' for NPC/monster actions ('the golem attacks').
claims.source: Dungeon Master Assistance — D&D 5E Writer's Guide (Ronny, 2015-08-03)
claims.quote: Wherever possible, avoid using the future tense

claims.claim: Justin Alexander: 2024 capitalizes defined terms (Cone, Target) to flag Rules Glossary entries, but definitions then live only in the glossary, scattering the targeting rules across pp. 236–238, 361, 364 and 376.
claims.source: The Alexandrian — D&D 5E 2024: Why Rules Glossaries Kinda Suck (2024-08-28)

claims.feature: teach-first structure and annotated play example (2024)
claims.claim: The 2024 PHB opens with a How to Play chapter and a two-column example of play annotated with the applicable rules; Crawford frames the rewrite as 'teaching you how to play', contrasting 2014 which 'jumps right into character creation'.
claims.source: Wargamer — New DnD Player's Handbook aims to actually teach you the game (2024-06-18)
claims.quote: teaching you how to play

claims.claim: Mearls' 2013 Legends & Lore argument, as quoted: feat names like 'Rapid Shot and Precise Shot are abstract things that aren't really clear', whereas describing a fighter as an archer 'makes sense to anyone'; rules are 'a shared language'.
claims.source: Tenkar's Tavern — Mike Mearls' Latest Legends & Lore Column: Where Less is More (2013-03-03)
claims.quote: a shared language

claims.claim: Perkins says every adventure for a decade had to re-explain doors, so the 2024 DMG codifies them; Wyatt calls re-explaining boxed text in every adventure a 'stupid little thing' the DMG (p. 9) now covers, pending the editing team.
claims.source: Screen Rant — After DM's Guide Preview, I'm Convinced Future D&D Adventures Will Drop These Two Repetitive Features (Ben Brosofsky, 2024-10-29)
claims.quote: stupid little thing

claims.feature: no dictated PC actions or emotions
claims.claim: Merwin's D&D Beyond rules: never 'as you approach' or 'you enter'; never 'stunned', 'terrified', 'heart pounds'; no game-mechanics terms used non-mechanically in boxed text.
claims.source: D&D Beyond — Let's Design an Adventure: Boxed Text (Shawn Merwin, 2019-11-06)

claims.feature: active voice and expletive cuts (editor via critic)
claims.claim: Vallese's book, per Lynch: cut 'there is/are' openings ('An old wise man watches over the children'), prefer active constructions, and reorder stacked modifiers ('Its wormlike body is thin and scaly').
claims.source: tenfootpole.org — Writing with Style: An Editor's Advice for RPG Writers review (Bryce Lynch, 2018-08-13)
claims.quote: Its wormlike body is thin and scaly

claims.claim: Gus L. rejects player-facing boxed text because it discourages referees from reading keys and is 'depreciating one big advantage RPGs have'.
claims.source: All Dead Generations — Dungeon Design, Process and Keys (Gus L., 2022-12-19)
claims.quote: depreciating one big advantage RPGs have

claims.claim: Gnome Stew (2008): in the 1980s reading boxed text aloud was 'considered a cardinal sin' among GMs, who were expected to paraphrase; the author later found reading helped immersion; commenters: 'Short box text is fine, long box text is a challenge.'
claims.source: Gnome Stew — Hot Button: Reading the Boxed Text (Walt Ciechanowski, 2008-12-18)
claims.quote: considered a cardinal sin

claims.claim: In 2005 WotC R&D was actively testing alternatives to boxed text at the table, to appear in products if they played better.
claims.source: Design & Development: Undercover at Gen Con, Part 1 (Jesse Decker & David Noonan, 2005-09-16)
claims.quote: We're goofing around with some alternatives right now.
claims.page: WotC designer column (read via Wayback text)

claims.claim: Pregenerated NPC stat blocks are no fun on a read-through but save the busy DM at the table, and WotC was working to make such material easier to find and use.
claims.source: Design & Development: Reads Bad, Plays Good (David Noonan, 2006-06-16)
claims.quote: They're no fun on a read-through.

claims.claim: RPGA/Living Greyhawk guidance forbids 'you', 'your' and 'you're' in read-aloud text because they seize control of the characters.
claims.source: Living Greyhawk, Intro to Writing: Dire Boxed Text (Craig Heir, RPGA/WotC, 2004-04-13)
claims.quote: Avoid the word "you" like the plague
claims.page: RPGA editor column on WotC site (read via Wayback)

claims.claim: Mechanics demand a lawyerly precision of language while setting text deliberately leaves gaps for the players' imagination.
claims.source: Mike Mearls of Dungeons & Dragons: Documenting Imaginary Worlds (SFWA, 2016-12-22)
claims.quote: a lawyerly approach to writing

claims.claim: Mearls' 2013 Legends & Lore column: rules terms exist to give abstract concepts a clear shared meaning, so '5th-level wizard' tells everyone what you can do.
claims.source: Legend & Lore says 'story not rules' (EN World thread quoting Mearls' 2013-03-04 column)
claims.quote: D&D is a shared language.

claims.claim: Mearls contrasts a self-explanatory descriptor like 'archer' with abstract feat names (Rapid Shot, Precise Shot) that can only be understood by already knowing them.
claims.source: Legend & Lore says 'story not rules' (EN World thread quoting Mearls' 2013-03-04 column)
claims.quote: They don't stand on their own in a meaningful way.

claims.claim: Wyatt set out to recapture the welcoming, teaching tone of the 4e DMG that the 2014 DMG lacked.
claims.source: D&D's James Wyatt & Chris Perkins Talk 2024 DM's Guide (CBR, 2024-10-25)
claims.quote: the helpful tone to ease you in

claims.claim: Wyatt wrote the 2024 DMG's examples of play as scripts of the game unfolding to show how it functions.
claims.source: D&D's James Wyatt & Chris Perkins Talk 2024 DM's Guide (CBR, 2024-10-25)
claims.quote: presenting the scripts of that unfolding in play

claims.claim: Every published WotC adventure opens by explaining what boxed text is; with the 2024 DMG defining it on p. 9, Wyatt wants to drop that boilerplate.
claims.source: After DM's Guide Preview, Future D&D Adventures Will Drop These Two Repetitive Features (Screen Rant, 2024-10-29)
claims.quote: tells you what boxed text is

claims.claim: Abadia (AL admin): dropping boxed text does not remove the need to tell the DM what to convey; the test is whether information reaches the DM.
claims.source: The Best and Worst of Adventure Formats at Winter Fantasy 2020 (Teos Abadia, Alphastream, 2020-02-20)
claims.quote: the DM still needs some way to understand what to convey

claims.claim: Baur (ex-Dungeon editor) says most history is wasted energy; keep backstory recent and relevant and avoid openings of 'Thousands of years ago'.
claims.source: Adventure Builder: Writing Your First Adventure, Part 1 of 6 (Wolfgang Baur, Wizards.com, 2006-07-28)
claims.quote: avoid anything that starts "Thousands of years ago..."

claims.claim: Monster entries are not allowed to break across page spreads, which limits text length and illustration size.
claims.source: Design & Development: How to Make a Monster Manual, Part 1 (David Noonan, 2007-07-27)
claims.quote: monsters don't break out of page spreads

claims.feature: headers and bullets for the DM's eye
claims.claim: Merwin: use headers, subheaders and bullets to draw the DM's eye to the right information at the right time.
claims.source: Let's Design an Adventure: Thinking Like a Designer (Shawn Merwin, D&D Beyond, 2020-03-25)
claims.quote: Use headers and subheaders to call out breaks in information

claims.claim: Goodman Games designer Burnside (2025) says boxed text must be short, evocative and helpful, and that his 2018 boxes carried too many distractions.
claims.source: Read aloud text in modules: What are folks opinions, page 10 (EN World, 2025)
claims.quote: short, evocative, and helpful to the DM and players
claims.page: forum (posts by a Goodman Games designer)

claims.claim: Editions are spelled out and lowercased ('fifth edition'), with 4E/5E abbreviations confined to tables, conversion documents, or informal text.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
claims.quote: We write “fifth edition,” for instance, not “5th Edition.”

claims.claim: v1.08a newly permits singular 'they/their' but tells writers to reach for it only when no other pleasing alternative exists.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
claims.quote: but don’t abuse this liberty

claims.claim: In 2019 'man' and 'woman' were reserved for humans only, so a dwarf is a 'male dwarf', never a 'dwarf man'.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
claims.quote: we write “male dwarf,” not “dwarf man”

claims.claim: Gendered suffixes are avoided ('priest', 'actor'); 'priestess'/'actress' survive only inside an in-world title or organization name.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
claims.quote: Avoid gender-specific suffixes whenever possible

claims.claim: Sidebars are rationed; any sidebar that must follow a specific passage to make sense should be folded into body text instead.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
claims.quote: The best sidebars can appear anywhere on a page

claims.claim: 'Magic' is the adjective for objects (magic item, magic sword); 'magical' for other things; 'magical item' is forbidden.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
claims.quote: “magic item” and its variants should never be “magical item.”

claims.claim: Men and women are depicted equally in all roles; sexist clichés (damsel, sexy barmaid) are banned, with orcs and Northlanders as the two exceptions.
claims.source: Forgotten Realms Style Guide (Wizards of the Coast, bundle document)
claims.quote: Avoid clichés that reinforce sexist

claims.feature: current AL requirement to follow the D&D Style Guide
claims.claim: The 2025 Dungeoncraft guide (v1.9c) requires the provided template and familiarity with the D&D Style Guide and DMsGuild content guidelines.
claims.source: D&D Adventurers League Dungeoncraft Design Guide v1.9c (effective May 2025, updated 2025-06-23)
claims.quote: You should be familiar with the D&D Style Guide

claims.claim: Mike Shea argues brevity is critical and that living creatures should be kept out of boxed text because they may not be there when read.
claims.source: Sage Advice archive: "What are your thoughts on boxed text?" thread (April 2019)
claims.quote: Brevity is critically important

claims.claim: Shawn Merwin notes most DMs want boxed text, so publishers keep providing it despite streamed play rarely using it.
claims.source: Sage Advice archive: "What are your thoughts on boxed text?" thread (April 2019)
claims.quote: WANT boxed text

claims.feature: no public style guide update since 2019
claims.claim: As of 2025-06-13 a DMs Guild creator asked whether the style guide had been updated for the 2024 rules or Chicago 18th; the thread had no reply, confirming the public document is still the 2019 release.
claims.source: D&D Beyond forums, "Is there an update to the D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing document yet?" (2025-06-13)

claims.claim: EN World's 2023 report of the Planescape Dungeoncraft update states adventures must use official templates and comply with the D&D Style Guide and DMsGuild Content Guidelines or face removal.
claims.source: EN World, "D&D Adventurers League Unveils New DungeonCraft Document with Planescape In Focus" (2023-11)

claims.claim: WotC's 2020-06-18 statement committed to sensitivity readers on sourcebooks and to reviewing reprints for racially insensitive text.
claims.source: Gizmodo/io9, "Dungeons & Dragons Team Announces New Plans to Address Racism in the Game" (James Whitbrook, 2020-06-18)
claims.quote: That's just not right, and it's not something we believe in.

claims.claim: Ray Winninger said only the text of Curse of Strahd was revised; art and tarokka cards were unchanged and the revised text went free to prior D&D Beyond owners.
claims.source: Gizmodo/io9, "D&D's Culturally Sensitive Strahd Revamp Is Here, But It Doesn't Go Far Enough" (Julie Muncy, 2020-07-27)
claims.quote: surgical changes

claims.claim: WotC's announcement described the revamp as including the latest errata and a revised depiction of the Vistani.
claims.source: Wikipedia, "Curse of Strahd" (fetched 2026-09-06), citing PC Gamer 2020-07
claims.quote: a revised depiction of the Vistani

claims.claim: Bryce Lynch lists boxed text among the things he does not want in an adventure module.
claims.source: Bryce Lynch, 'Review Standards', tenfootpole.org
claims.quote: Boxed text is usually not a good thing.

claims.claim: Lynch asks for a web of stated relationships among a town's named residents so the place exists apart from the party.
claims.source: Bryce Lynch, tenfootpole.org
claims.quote: a web of personal relationships between the various people living in town

claims.claim: Hartlage names sunset colour as the type of unimportant ornament too many boxed descriptions dwell on.
claims.source: David Hartlage, DMDavid
claims.quote: the color of the sunset and other bits of obviously unimportant fluff

claims.claim: Alexander's key structure puts the seen-at-a-glance block first and requires it to hold everything conveyed on entering, before checks and before element-by-element detail.
claims.source: Justin Alexander, 'The Art of the Key – Part 2', The Alexandrian
claims.quote: contain all of the information that should be immediately conveyed

claims.claim: Hartlage notes that the 1999 introductory modules printed scripted text for the DM to read to new players.
claims.source: David Hartlage, DMDavid, 30 Jan 2024, on Eye of the Wyvern (1999)
claims.quote: scripted text for the DM to read to new players

claims.claim: A scholarly case study lists read-aloud text, player handouts, DM instructions and NPC dialogue among the five textual elements that carry an adventure's ideas.
claims.source: Brian McKenzie, Bret Zawilski and James Beirne, International Journal of Role-Playing 17, 2026
claims.quote: read-aloud text, player handouts, instructions to the Dungeon Master

claims.claim: The phrase 'succinct and evocative' on tenfootpole.org is the top grade for Language on a second reviewer's rating scale (signed 'The Pretty Girl'), not a line of Bryce Lynch's own standards.
claims.source: 'The Pretty Girl' (second reviewer), rating scale on tenfootpole.org 'Review Standards'
claims.quote: Succinct and evocative
claims.page: Review Standards, 'The Pretty Girl' scale, Language 4

claims.claim: Justin Alexander's prescribed key opens with the information a character perceives on entering, which he calls seen in a glance.
claims.source: Justin Alexander, 'The Art of the Key - Part 2', The Alexandrian, 2014
claims.quote: seen in a glance

claims.claim: In the same account Gygax credited a lifelong love of dictionaries and thesauruses for his vocabulary.
claims.source: James Maliszewski relaying a private conversation with Gary Gygax, 'High Gygaxian', Grognardia, 2009
claims.quote: his lifelong love of dictionaries and thesauruses

claims.claim: Bryce Lynch says the number one complaint about published adventures is that they are hard to run.
claims.source: Bryce Lynch, 'The Book Introduction', tenfootpole.org
claims.quote: The number one complaint about published adventures

claims.claim: Courtney Campbell's key format admits no word that is not important.
claims.source: Courtney Campbell, 'On Set Design', Hack & Slash, 2012
claims.quote: Any word that is not important, is not used.

claims.claim: Brendan of Necropraxis objects that Courtney Campbell's outline key, though usable, lacks poetry.
claims.source: Brendan (Necropraxis), 'Improved area keys', 2013
claims.quote: it lacks poetry

claims.claim: Reviewing a 2006 DCC module, Gabor Lux says much boxed text and follow-up writing are expended to say relatively little.
claims.source: Gabor Lux (Melan), '[REVIEW] Halls of the Minotaur', Beyond Fomalhaut, 2018
claims.quote: much boxed text and followup writing are expended to say relatively little

claims.claim: Howard contrasts OD&D's Sample Level, a collection of examples, with Holmes presenting his dungeon as part of a coherent adventure.
claims.source: Zach Howard (Zenopus Archives), 'Part 46', 2015
claims.quote: presents his dungeon ideas as part of a coherent adventure

claims.claim: The writeup says GAZ1's chapter of place descriptions is meant mostly for players rather than the DM.
claims.source: Rulebook Heavily, 'Dungeons & Dragons Gazetteer' writeup, RPG Writeups
claims.quote: The descriptions in this chapter are mostly meant for players
claims.page: Gaz 1 Part 4: The Lay of the Land

claims.claim: Deterding and Zagal credit Peterson and Appelcline, independent authors, with the substantial historiographies of tabletop role-playing games.
claims.source: Sebastian Deterding and Jose P. Zagal, 'The Many Faces of Role-Playing Game Studies', in Role-Playing Game Studies (Routledge 2018)
claims.quote: have produced substantial historiographies of the emergence and evolution
claims.page: section on the history of RPG studies
claims.routeHint: White Rose accepted-manuscript PDF, pypdf text extraction

claims.claim: Carbonell says role-playing gametexts appeared to him an overlooked area of investigation for literary scholars.
claims.source: Curtis D. Carbonell, interviewed on the Liverpool University Press blog, 2020
claims.quote: an overlooked area of investigation for literary scholars

claims.claim: Carbonell says forty years of published role-playing material was waiting to be mined by a literary scholar.
claims.source: Curtis D. Carbonell, interviewed on the Liverpool University Press blog, 2020
claims.quote: forty years of published material was out there, waiting to be mined

verdicts.trueWording: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing
verdicts.note: COMPLETENESS CRITIC §1: 'Seven VERBATIM rows carry a limb the verifier says is not on the page: [0] provenance...' Verifier's own caveat: 'the document itself says nothing about distribution to freelancers/Adventurers League authors or later DMs Guild bundling - that provenance is unverified by the source (only circumstantial: the host is adventurersleague.wordpress.com). Also "governs mechanics of style, not prose voice" is nearly but not wholly true: a "High Fantasy" section gives tone guidance.'
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: the distribution-to-freelancers/Adventurers-League and later DMs-Guild-bundling provenance is nowhere in the document, and the 'governs mechanics of style, not prose voice' half is contradicted by the guide's own High Fantasy tone section

verdicts.trueWording: The Chicago Manual of Style, 16th edition
verdicts.note: REGRADE (re-verification chunk, v1.08a): the January-2019 revision reads 'The Chicago Manual of Style, 17th edition', reversing the 16th-edition rule this row states as house law.
